Section 3.2 of Lock⁵ asks what a **confidence interval** really says. An interval estimate,
$\text{statistic} \pm \text{margin of error}$, gives a **range of plausible values** for the
population parameter: values inside the interval are consistent with the sample data, values
outside it are not. The **margin of error** measures how accurate the estimate is likely to be
— for a symmetric, bell-shaped sampling distribution it is about $2 \times SE$, half the width
of a 95% interval. Crucially, the **95% confidence refers to the method, not to any single
interval**: if we took many samples and built an interval from each, about 95% of those
intervals would capture the true parameter — but we never know whether *our* one interval is
among the lucky ones. There is also a **precision–confidence trade-off**: narrower intervals
are more precise but less reliable, while a higher confidence level widens the interval. The
way to get both precision *and* confidence is a **larger sample**, which shrinks the standard
error and hence the margin of error.
The exercises below are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data* (Lock⁵, 3rd ed.,
pp. 242–247). Skill Builders 3.43–3.58 practice parameter/statistic notation, building
intervals from a statistic and a margin of error, judging plausible parameter values, and
turning standard errors into intervals; 3.59–3.79 apply the ideas to real studies. None of
these exercises draw on a named Lock5 dataset, so the executable cells below simply recompute
the printed numbers, and simulate where the book invites technology (Exercise 3.78).

## Exercise 3.43

estimate.)* A random sample of registered voters in the US is used to estimate the
proportion of all US registered voters who voted in the last election.

- **(a) Parameter:** $p$ = the proportion of **all US registered voters** who voted in the

## Exercise 3.59

**What Proportion of College Students Change Their Major?** A survey of 5204 first-year
full-time college students in the US, administered at the end of the first year, found that
35.6% had changed their choice of major during the year.

- **(a) Sample.** The 5204 students are a subset of all US first-year full-time college
  students.
- **(b) Statistic**, $\hat{p} = 0.356$ — it describes the sample.
- **(c) Parameter:** $p$ = the proportion of **all US first-year full-time college students**
  who change their choice of major during the first year.
- **(d)** $\hat{p} \pm 2 \cdot SE = 0.356 \pm 2(0.007) = 0.356 \pm 0.014$: the 95% confidence
  interval is **0.342 to 0.370**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
phat, se = 0.356, 0.007
pd.Series({"Best estimate": phat, "Margin of error": 2 * se,
           "95% CI": f"({phat - 2*se:.3f}, {phat + 2*se:.3f})"}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.61

**Adolescent Brains Are Different.** Participants first learned to associate fear with a
particular sound, then their ability to "unlearn" the connection was measured (larger
numbers indicate less fear). We estimate the difference in mean response between adults and
teenagers: mean response 0.225 for adults, 0.059 for teenagers, standard error 0.091.

- **(a)** $\mu_A - \mu_T$ = the difference in mean physiological fear response between all
  adults and all teenagers (adults minus teenagers).
- **(b)** $\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_T = 0.225 - 0.059 = \mathbf{0.166}$.
- **(c)** $0.166 \pm 2(0.091) = 0.166 \pm 0.182$: the 95% confidence interval is
  **−0.016 to 0.348**.
- **(d) An experiment** — the fear association was deliberately created by the researchers
  as part of the study protocol (although the adult/teen comparison itself was not
  randomized: age is pre-existing).

```{python}
#| echo: false
est, se = 0.225 - 0.059, 0.091
pd.Series({"Best estimate": round(est, 3), "Margin of error": round(2 * se, 3),
           "95% CI": f"({est - 2*se:.3f}, {est + 2*se:.3f})"}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.63

**Do You Prefer Pain over Solitude?** In a second study, 12 of 18 men and 6 of 24 women
voluntarily gave themselves at least one electric shock rather than sit in solitary thought;
the standard error of the estimate is 0.154.

- **(a)** $p_M - p_W$ = the difference in the proportion of **all** men and **all** women
  (like those in the study) who would prefer pain over solitude (men minus women).
- **(b)** $\hat{p}_M - \hat{p}_W = 12/18 - 6/24 = 0.667 - 0.250 = \mathbf{0.417}$.
- **(c)** $0.417 \pm 2(0.154) = 0.417 \pm 0.308$: the 95% confidence interval is
  **0.109 to 0.725**.
- **(d) No.** Zero is not in the interval, so "no difference" between males and females is
  not plausible — men are more likely to prefer pain over solitude.

```{python}
#| echo: false
est = 12/18 - 6/24
se = 0.154
pd.Series({"p-hat (men)": round(12/18, 3), "p-hat (women)": round(6/24, 3),
           "Best estimate": round(est, 3),
           "95% CI": f"({est - 2*se:.3f}, {est + 2*se:.3f})"}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.64

**Moose Drool Makes Grass More Appetizing.** One grass species produces the toxin
ergovaline (about 1.0 ppm) to deter grazers; saliva from a moose counteracts the toxin.
Scientists estimate that, after treatment with moose drool, the mean ergovaline level on the
grass is 0.183 ppm, with standard error 0.016.

- **(a)** $\mu$ = the mean level of ergovaline (in ppm) on grass **after treatment with
  moose drool** (for all such grass).
- **(b)** $\bar{x} = \mathbf{0.183}$ ppm.
- **(c)** $0.183 \pm 2(0.016) = 0.183 \pm 0.032$: the 95% confidence interval is
  **0.151 to 0.215 ppm**. We are 95% sure that the mean toxin level on drool-treated grass
  is between 0.151 and 0.215 ppm — far below the roughly 1.0 ppm without treatment, so moose
  saliva does appear to make the grass more appetizing.

```{python}
#| echo: false
est, se = 0.183, 0.016
pd.Series({"Best estimate": est, "Margin of error": round(2 * se, 3),
           "95% CI": f"({est - 2*se:.3f}, {est + 2*se:.3f})"}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.67

**Subtle Language Changes Impact Conflict Resolution.** Participants were randomly divided
into two groups hearing controversial statements in noun form (Group 1) or verb form
(Group 2), then rated their anger on a 1–6 scale. A 90% confidence interval for the
difference in mean anger rating (Group 1 − Group 2) is −0.86 to −0.06.

- **(a)** $\mu_N - \mu_V$ = the difference in mean anger rating between all people hearing
  statements in **noun form** and all people hearing them in **verb form**.
- **(b)** $\bar{x}_N - \bar{x}_V$ — the midpoint of the interval:
  $(-0.86 + (-0.06))/2 = \mathbf{-0.46}$ (matching Exercise 2.82).
- **(c) No.** Zero is not in the interval, so "basically the same" mean anger is not
  plausible at the 90% level. The interval is entirely negative, so the **noun form has the
  lower mean anger** and the verb form the higher.
- **(d) Yes** — participants were **randomly assigned** to a language form, so the
  difference in anger can be attributed to the language structure itself.
- **(e) Yes, it matters:** to keep anger low, use the **noun form** ("the division of
  Jerusalem" rather than "dividing Jerusalem").

```{python}
#| echo: false
mid = (-0.86 + -0.06) / 2
pd.Series({"Best estimate": mid, "90% CI": "(-0.86, -0.06)",
           "Zero plausible?": bool(-0.86 <= 0 <= -0.06)}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.68

**Soda Consumption and Mortality in Europe.** A hazard ratio of 1 means no discernible
difference in risk between groups. In a large European study, the hazard ratio for mortality
for people drinking two or more glasses of soda per day (relative to less than one glass a
month) was 1.17, with 95% confidence interval 1.11 to 1.22.

- **(a) Yes.** The entire interval lies **above 1**, so with 95% confidence, high soda
  consumption is associated with an increased risk of death.
- **(b) No.** This is an **observational study** — soda consumption was not assigned — so
  association does not imply causation; confounding variables (diet, lifestyle, weight...)
  could explain the association.

## Exercise 3.69

**Is a Car a Necessity?** A random sample of $n = 1483$ US adults found a 95% confidence
interval of 0.83 to 0.89 for the proportion saying a car is a necessity.

- **Correct interpretation:** We are 95% confident that the **proportion of all US adults**
  who consider a car a necessity is **between 0.83 and 0.89** — these are the plausible
  values of the parameter.
- It does *not* mean 95% of adults say "necessity", nor that 95% of future samples fall in
  this interval, nor anything about individual people — the interval estimates one
  population proportion, and the 95% describes the reliability of the *method*.

## Exercise 3.71

**What Proportion Believe in One True Love?** In Data 2.1, a random sample of 2625 US
adults was asked whether there is "only one true love for each person"; 735 agreed. The
standard error for this sample proportion is 0.009.

- **Parameter:** $p$ = the proportion of all US adults who agree that there is only one true
  love for each person.
- **Best estimate:** $\hat{p} = 735/2625 = \mathbf{0.28}$.
- **Margin of error:** $2(0.009) = \mathbf{0.018}$.
- **95% confidence interval:** $0.28 \pm 0.018$ = **0.262 to 0.298**. We are 95% confident
  that between about 26.2% and 29.8% of all US adults believe there is only one true love.

```{python}
#| echo: false
phat = 735 / 2625
se = 0.009
pd.Series({"n": 2625, "Best estimate": round(phat, 3),
           "Margin of error": round(2 * se, 3),
           "95% CI": f"({phat - 2*se:.3f}, {phat + 2*se:.3f})"}).to_string()
```

| Disagree | 807 | 1005 | 1812 |
| Don't know | 34 | 44 | 78 |
| Total | 1213 | 1412 | 2625 |

Using the fact that the standard error for the difference is 0.018, the 95% confidence
interval for $p_M - p_F$ is $\hat{p}_M - \hat{p}_F \pm 2(0.018) = 0.0496 \pm 0.036$, i.e.
**0.014 to 0.086**.

- **Interpretation:** We are 95% confident that the proportion of males agreeing exceeds the
  proportion of females agreeing by between 1.4 and 8.6 percentage points.

  between males and females; males are somewhat more likely to agree.

## Exercise 3.73

**Playing Video Games.** 23 male volunteers: 11 action video game players, 12 non-players.
A 95% confidence interval for mean response time, players minus non-players, is −1.8 to
−1.2 seconds; for mean accuracy score, players minus non-players, it is −4.2 to +5.8.

- **(a)** We are 95% confident that the mean response time for game players is between 1.2
  and 1.8 seconds **lower** than for non-players (the interval for players − non-players is
  entirely negative).
- **(b) Not plausible.** Zero is not in the interval, so the groups are not basically the
  same in response time — **game players are faster** (smaller response time).
- **(c)** We are 95% confident that the mean accuracy score for game players is between 4.2
  points lower and 5.8 points higher than for non-players.
- **(d) Plausible.** Zero is in the interval, so the groups may be basically the same in
  accuracy; if they do differ, the interval does not even tell us which group is more
  accurate.

## Exercise 3.74

**Bisphenol A in Your Soup Cans.** 75 participants ate canned soup or fresh soup for lunch
for five days, switched groups after a break, and the difference in urinary BPA between the
two treatments was measured for each participant. A 95% confidence interval for the
difference in means (canned minus fresh) is 19.6 to 25.5 μg/L.

- **(a) A matched pairs experiment.** Each participant experienced **both** treatments (in
  sequence), so each person serves as their own control — this removes person-to-person
  variability in baseline BPA. (It is an experiment because the diet was imposed.)
- **(b)** $\mu_d$ = the mean difference in urinary BPA concentration (canned minus fresh)
  for the population of participants like these.
- **(c)** The entire interval is positive: we are 95% confident that canned soup
  consumption raises mean urinary BPA by between 19.6 and 25.5 μg/L — consistent with the
  reported "more than 1000% increase."
- **(d) Narrower.** With 500 participants instead of 75 the standard error would shrink
  (roughly by a factor of $\sqrt{500/75}$), so the margin of error — and the interval —
  would be smaller.

## Exercise 3.75

**Predicting Election Results.** For each poll, the candidate wins with confidence only if
their interval lies **entirely above 50%** (and above the opponent's interval):

```{python}
#| echo: false
polls = pd.DataFrame({"Poll": list("abcd"),
                      "A": [54, 52, 53, 58], "B": [46, 48, 47, 42],
                      "ME": [5, 1, 2, 10]})
rows = []
for _, r in polls.iterrows():
    a_lo, a_hi = r["A"] - r["ME"], r["A"] + r["ME"]
    b_lo, b_hi = r["B"] - r["ME"], r["B"] + r["ME"]
    rows.append({"Poll": r["Poll"], "A interval": f"({a_lo}, {a_hi})",
                 "B interval": f"({b_lo}, {b_hi})",
                 "Intervals overlap": a_lo <= b_hi,
                 "A entirely above 50%": a_lo > 50,
                 "Confident A wins": (a_lo > 50) and not (a_lo <= b_hi)})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Poll").to_string()
```

- **(a) Not confident.** A: 54 ± 5 = (49, 59); B: 46 ± 5 = (41, 51). The intervals overlap
  and A's dips below 50%.
- **(b) Confident.** A: (51, 53); B: (47, 49). No overlap, and all of A's interval is above
  50%.
- **(c) Confident.** A: (51, 55); B: (45, 49). No overlap, A entirely above 50%.
- **(d) Not confident.** A: (48, 68); B: (32, 52). The intervals overlap (48 to 52), so B
  could still win.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Poll intervals for candidates A and B in each of the four polls, with the 50 percent line
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
for i, (_, r) in enumerate(polls.iterrows()):
    ax.errorbar(i - 0.15, r["A"], yerr=r["ME"], fmt="o", color="#4c72b0",
                capsize=4, label="Candidate A" if i == 0 else "")
    ax.errorbar(i + 0.15, r["B"], yerr=r["ME"], fmt="o", color="#c44e52",
                capsize=4, label="Candidate B" if i == 0 else "")
ax.axhline(50, color="gray", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.text(3.42, 50.4, "50%", color="gray", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xticks(range(4), ["(a) ±5", "(b) ±1", "(c) ±2", "(d) ±10"])
ax.set_xlabel("Poll (margin of error)")
ax.set_ylabel("Support (%)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 3.76

**Effect of Overeating for One Month: Average Long-Term Weight Gain.** 18 healthy,
normal-weight people increased calorie intake by 70% and limited activity for four weeks.
Two and a half years later, the mean weight gain for participants was 6.8 lbs with a
standard error of 1.2 lbs (a control group that did not binge had no change).

- **(a)** $\mu$ = the **mean weight gain two and a half years later** for all people (like
  these) who overeat for a month.
- **(b)** The exact value could only be found with a **census** — measuring the weight gain
  2.5 years later for *everyone* in the population — which is impractical; that is why we
  estimate with a confidence interval.
- **(c)** $6.8 \pm 2(1.2) = 6.8 \pm 2.4$: the 95% confidence interval is **4.4 to 9.2
  lbs**. We are 95% sure that, on average, people who overeat for a month gain between 4.4
  and 9.2 pounds two and a half years later.
- **(d)** Margin of error $= 2(1.2) = \mathbf{2.4}$ lbs: our best estimate of 6.8 lbs is
  likely within about 2.4 lbs of the true population mean.

```{python}
#| echo: false
est, se = 6.8, 1.2
pd.Series({"Best estimate": est, "Margin of error": 2 * se,
           "95% CI": f"({est - 2*se:.1f}, {est + 2*se:.1f})"}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.77

**Fluoride Exposure in Pregnant Women.** Regression lines predicting children's IQ scores
from maternal fluoride concentration were fit separately for boys and girls; the effect
seems real for boys but inconclusive for girls. The two 95% confidence intervals for the
slope are −2.53 to 7.33 and −8.38 to −0.60.

- **Boys: −8.38 to −0.60.** This interval is entirely negative — a negative slope (more
  fluoride ↔ lower IQ) is detected, matching the "true for boys" conclusion.
- **Girls: −2.53 to 7.33.** This interval contains 0, so a slope of 0 (no effect) remains
  plausible — matching the "inconclusive for girls" conclusion.

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.Series({"Boys": "(-8.38, -0.60) — excludes 0: significant negative slope",
           "Girls": "(-2.53, 7.33) — includes 0: inconclusive"}).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.78

**What Proportion of Canadian Adults Are Married?** The 2016 Canadian Census shows
$p = 0.457$ of Canadian adults are married. Draw samples of size $n = 100$ (as StatKey
would) and build each 95% interval as $\hat{p} \pm 2(0.050)$:

- **(a)** The simulation below draws sample proportions: with the fixed seed shown, the
  first sample gives $\hat{p} = \mathbf{0.42}$ (your value will differ — that is the point).
- **(b)** $0.42 \pm 0.10$: interval **0.320 to 0.520**.
- **(c) Yes** — $p = 0.457$ is inside this interval (the method worked this time).
- **(d)** A second sample gives $\hat{p} = \mathbf{0.47}$, interval **0.370 to 0.570**, which
  also contains 0.457 — but any single interval may miss; about 95% of such intervals
  capture $p$.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
rows = []
for k in range(2):
    phat = rng.choice([1, 0], size=100, p=[0.457, 0.543]).mean()
    lo, hi = phat - 2 * 0.050, phat + 2 * 0.050
    rows.append({"Sample": k + 1, "p-hat": phat,
                 "95% CI": f"({lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f})",
                 "Contains p = 0.457?": bool(lo <= 0.457 <= hi)})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("Sample").to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.79

**Student Misinterpretations.** The data are pulse rates from a random sample of 100
students at *her college*, and the 95% confidence interval for the mean pulse rate is
(65.5, 71.8). The **correct** interpretation is: *we are 95% confident that the mean pulse
rate for all students at this college is between 65.5 and 71.8 beats per minute.* Each
statement below is improper:

- **(a)** Speaks of **all students' individual pulse rates** — the interval estimates the
  *mean*, not every individual value.
- **(b)** Speaks of the mean **for this sample** — the sample mean is known exactly (68.65,
  the center of the interval); no estimation needed.
- **(c)** We are 100% sure the interval goes from 65.5 to 71.8 — it was *computed* to do so;
  the 95% describes how often the *method* captures the parameter, not the interval itself.
- **(d)** "95% of all students" — again confuses an interval for the **mean** with an
  interval for **individual** pulse rates.
- **(e)** Wrong **population**: the sample came from *this college*, not all US college
  students.
- **(f)** Individual students do not have "mean pulse rates" — the statement garbles what
  quantity is being estimated (the population mean, one fixed number).
- **(g)** Closest to right, but still improper: 95% of sample means fall within $2 \times SE$
  of the **population mean** $\mu$, not within this one fixed interval centered at
  $\bar{x} = 68.65$; the interval (65.5, 71.8) either captures $\mu$ or it does not.

:::
